cards.explanation: The answer is False. God says, "I am jealous for Zion with great zeal; I am jealous for her with great fervor." He says it twice, first with zeal and then with fervor. I think that's a God leaning in toward Zion, not walking away from her.

The answer is that God will return and dwell in Jerusalem. He says, "I will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem." The One returning is the LORD Himself, friends. Then Jerusalem gets a brand new name, which is coming up.

The answer is the Holy Mountain. God says, "…the mountain of the LORD of Hosts will be called the Holy Mountain." Jerusalem gets the name City of Truth, and the mountain gets its own name too. A city and a mountain, each with a new name.

The answer is that they will sit along the streets. God says, "Old men and old women will again sit along the streets of Jerusalem, each with a staff in hand because of great age." Notice the word "again," friends. Sitting along the streets is the whole picture here.

The answer is playing. God says, "…the streets of the city will be filled with boys and girls playing there." So the old folks sit on the streets, and the young ones play right alongside them. That's a lot of life in one city, friends.

The answer is that it isn't impossible for Him. God asks, "…should it also be impossible in My eyes?" The way He asks it, the answer is no, friends. Right after that He keeps going with "I will save My people…" (Zechariah 8:7).

The answer is True. God says, "I will bring them back to dwell in Jerusalem, where they will be My people, and I will be their faithful and righteous God." Two promises are packed in there, friends: the bringing back and the being their God. I wish every sentence of mine came with that much in it.

The answer is "Let your hands be strong." God says, "Let your hands be strong, you who now hear these words spoken by the prophets who were present when the foundations were laid to rebuild the temple…" He's talking to people who have work in front of them. And strong hands are exactly what any work needs, even stamping cookies.

The answer is True, and it's a heavy one. God says that before those days, "…neither man nor beast received wages, nor was there safety from the enemy for anyone who came or went, for I had turned every man against his neighbor." That's a hard picture of how things were, friends. The next verse starts with "But now," and that's where the hope is.

The answer is that their crops will thrive. God says, "…the seed will be prosperous, the vine will yield its fruit, the ground will yield its produce, and the skies will give their dew." Then He says He'll give all of it to the remnant as an inheritance, friends. It's a promise that the land will answer them.

The answer is blessing. God says, "As you have been a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you will be a blessing." Same people, but a flip from curse to blessing, friends. Then He adds, "Do not be afraid; let your hands be strong."

The answer is False. God says, "Just as I resolved to bring disaster upon you when your fathers provoked Me to anger, and I did not relent…" The part that doesn't fit is the relenting, friends, because the text says He did not. It's a heavy verse, and the next one turns toward good.

The answer is that He has resolved to do good again to Jerusalem and Judah. God says, "so now I have resolved to do good again to Jerusalem and Judah." He resolved on disaster back then and didn't relent, friends. Now He says He has resolved on good, and then adds, "Do not be afraid…"

The answer is speaking truth to one another. God says, "These are the things you must do: Speak truth to one another, render true and sound judgments in your gates…" The list starts with plain honest talk between people, friends. I like a list where the first item is something you can do before breakfast.

The answer is hates. God says, "…do not plot evil in your hearts against your neighbor, and do not love to swear falsely, for I hate all these things…" He doesn't say He tolerates them or shrugs, friends. He says hate, and then He signs it, "declares the LORD…"

The answer is times of joy and gladness. God says the fasts of the fourth, the fifth, the seventh and the tenth months "…will become times of joy and gladness, cheerful feasts for the house of Judah." Those four fasts get a whole new meaning, friends. And this is how the passage answers the fasting question from the beginning (Zechariah 7:3).

The answer is truth and peace. God says, "Therefore you are to love both truth and peace." It comes right after the promise that the fasts become cheerful feasts, friends. So the joy comes, and He tells them what to love.

The answer is "Let us go and seek the LORD." The residents of one city will go to another, saying, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." They don't say it to themselves, friends. They say it to the people in the other city.

The answer is True. The ones doing the inviting say, "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." Then they add, "I myself am going." That's not a "you go ahead, I'll catch up later," friends. They're in.

The answer is False. God says, "…many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the LORD of Hosts in Jerusalem and to plead before the LORD." He says many peoples, and He says strong nations, friends. That's a big crowd, and it's nothing like a few small nations.

The answer is "We have heard that God is with you." Ten men from the nations say, "Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you." Their reason is what they've heard about God being with them, friends. It's a lovely way to end the chapter, and I mean that.
